De nombreuses femmes en Iran prennent le: Many women in Iran are taking to the streets, removing their veils, burning them and sometimes cutting their hair. In Quebec, several Muslim teachers are challenging Bill 21, which prevents them from wearing the veil. Illustration: Nia E-K
« Une nouvelle révolution a-t-elle comme: “Has a new revolution begun?”, “A revolution under way”, “A turning point in Iran”. These headlines have followed one another in the United States, France and Canada since the death of Mahsa Zhina Amini on September 16. The world is watching and commenting on the actions of these Iranian women who are demanding an end to mandatory veiling.
Au Québec, la situation réveille des déb: In Quebec, the situation has reawakened divisive, perennial debates. Wearing the veil is being widely questioned, and the issue is more heated than ever. Faced with a torrent of comments and sub-debates, it is easy to forget the real issue, the Iranian women’s primary demand: women’s right to self-determination. And what if, to support these women, all it took was to listen to them and “leave them alone”?
« C’était choquant, j’ai beaucoup pleuré: “It was shocking, I cried a lot. I pictured myself in her place, so young and innocent,” recalls Setareh Sadeqi, who holds a doctorate in American studies and is an independent public policy researcher, teacher and translator, speaking from her office in Isfahan, Iran. Mahsa Zhina (her Kurdish first name) Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish student, died on September 16 in Tehran while in the custody of the morality police (“guidance police” in Farsi) for wearing her scarf improperly.
Instauré à la suite de la révolution isl: Introduced after the 1979 Islamic Revolution by Ayatollah Khomeini, wearing the veil is mandatory for women and girls over the age of nine. Punishments for violations range from arrest to beatings and flogging, as well as time in prison. “It’s unacceptable to be treated like this,” Ms. Sadeqi continues in a measured voice.
La mort de Zhina est l’étincelle qui a e: Zhina’s death is the spark that set Iran ablaze. Many women are taking the country’s streets by storm, removing their veils, sometimes burning them. They are calling for an end to mandatory veiling and to the morality police. Men, boys and families are joining them. Very quickly, the demands evolve and diversify, and with them comes a very strong call to overthrow the regime. Workers and shopkeepers are doing the same. The state has responded by cracking down on the protests, but also by blocking Internet access, <l1>notably in Kurdistan and Sistan and Baluchestan</l1>.
Au nom de Mahsa Amini, on peut ajouter c: To the name of Mahsa Amini, we can add those of Hananeh Kian, 23, Mahsa Mogoi, 18, Ghazaleh Chalab, 32, and at least 180 other adults and children killed during the protests, <l1>according to the latest figures from Iran Human Rights (IHR)</l1>.
Le sujet devient viral sur les réseaux s: The subject goes viral on social media, and the media seize on it. Newspapers and magazines around the world quickly announce a “revolution under way” in Iran. For Ms. Sadeqi, the situation is more nuanced. “There’s a lot of exaggeration,” she cautions, explaining that these protests are unique, but they didn’t come out of nowhere either.
Le corps de la femme est instrumentalisé: Women’s bodies have long been instrumentalized in Iran. Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi had banned the veil in 1921. “SAVAK, the secret political police of the time, would rip the veil off women’s heads,” says Hanieh Ziaei, an Iranologist affiliated with UQAM’s Raoul-Dandurand Chair. Since the Islamic Revolution and the imposition of the veil, women have regularly revolted to try to regain their rights, as with the #MercredisBlancs in 2017 and through a multitude of feminist movements and campaigns organized over the years. “The veil was torn from them, then imposed on them, without anyone asking their opinion,” sums up Hanieh Ziaei.
En outre, la population ne reste pas non: Moreover, the population has not stayed silent in the face of the economic crisis, religious and political ideology, and corruption. In 2019, the working class rose up against rising fuel prices and the stifling economic situation; 1,500 protesters were killed.
« Cela n’a pas eu une grande couverture,: “That didn’t get much coverage, even though workers matter! In terms of numbers, today is nowhere near the 2019 protests,” says Setareh Sadeqi, noting that the Toronto demonstration drew more supporters.
« En revanche, cette année, c’est la pre: “On the other hand, this year is the first time that women are at the forefront,” she acknowledges. Besides the famous “Woman, Life, Freedom” (a Kurdish slogan from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), for whom the revolution was to be made with women) chanted and taken up everywhere, protesters are also shouting “Death to the dictator” and “Death to the regime”. This has become a key demand of the protests.
Hana – qui préfère taire son nom de fami: Hana, who prefers not to give her last name, is wary of Western media and wanted to make sure our approach was sound before agreeing to speak. Saying she is “proud to be an Iranian woman,” she fervently confirms that the situation is more nuanced than the picture the media paint.
Originaire du sud-ouest du pays, Hana se: Originally from the southwest of the country, Hana describes herself as “half Arab, half Persian”. After living in Australia for eight years, she returned to her native country last summer without a hijab. She didn’t wear one in Australia and wanted to keep it that way in Iran. “A lot of people warned me, but I didn’t listen to them, I wanted to fight for my freedom,” she explains from her apartment in Tehran, the country’s capital.
Elle aussi a déjà été arrêtée et interro: She, too, has already been arrested and questioned. But before Mahsa Amini’s death, she walked the streets of Tehran without a veil. And everything went fine. She says she saw far fewer police officers than eight years ago. “It’s not just me playing the hero by not wearing the hijab. Change is happening fast in Iran, women are daring to make changes for themselves,” she says loudly and firmly.
Hana n’a pas encore participé aux manife: Hana has not yet taken part in the protests. “I just went to watch one. I regret that the protests are scattered, with no clear message, or sometimes organized by groups whose values I reject,” the young woman shares.
Elle se méfie des groupes « séparatistes: She is wary of the “separatist and terrorist” groups that are organizing the protests, but also of groups that tolerate or call for foreign interference. “I would take part in a protest tomorrow if the call came from other groups, and if the protest called for an end to mandatory hijab and an end to the morality police,” she states.
Pour comprendre les manifestations actue: To understand the current protests, we also have to look at the different demands and understand the multitude of interest groups. Starting with local and regional groups, which, as in any movement, are numerous and each have their own agenda.
Comme le fait Hana en sélectionnant les: Like Hana, who chooses which media outlets she speaks to, journalist and lecturer Shenaz Kermalli, who teaches at Toronto Metropolitan University and the University of Toronto, recommends being careful about disinformation and about the sources we listen to and use. On her social media, she warns internet users about what they read, as many others do.
Au-delà de l’influence de ces groupes et: Beyond the influence of these groups and the information war, as a <l1>CNN</l1> article explains, Ms. Kermalli is also studying Western media coverage of the protests.
Depuis le 16 septembre, la diaspora se m: Since September 16, the diaspora has mobilized and organized impressive marches, such as the one that <l1>brought together 50,000 people in Toronto on October 1</l1>. At the same time, diaspora figures are speaking out in outrage and using their influence to talk about the situation, such as the controversial journalist Masih Alinejad. Many political, media and cultural figures of all backgrounds are joining the movement and <l2>filming themselves cutting their hair</l2>.
Face à un tel soutien international, les: Faced with such international support, the women we spoke to all wonder why it is in 2022 that the world is listening to Iranian women. “The 2019 uprisings didn’t draw this much attention; why does it take a burned scarf for people to talk about it?” asks Shenaz Kermalli.
Certains y voient une conséquence du mou: Some see it as a consequence of the #MeToo movement, which turned five in October and which is thought to have started a loosening of tongues, but also created more space to talk about sexist and sexual violence and patriarchy. The influence of regional and international actors is often pointed to: Saudi Arabia, for example, but also the United States or Israel.
Pour Mme Kermalli, la couverture médiati: For Ms. Kermalli, Canadian media coverage resembles American coverage. “There’s a tendency to follow along on Middle East politics. Mainstream media tend to cover Middle Eastern and Asian issues with less scepticism and criticism,” she explains. A good example is the war in Iraq, whose poor Western coverage is studied in journalism schools, the media having relied on reports from news agencies. “When we do that, we’re not helping the people on the ground,” concludes Ms. Kermalli.
Cette illustration représente la solidar: This illustration depicts solidarity among women who are fed up with not having a choice over their bodies and their voices, in Quebec as in Iran. Illustration: Nia E-K
Parmi les raisons pouvant expliquer l’in: Among the reasons that may explain Western media interest is also the veil. The hijab is a hot-button subject in many societies. In France, for example, the protests in Iran are exacerbating the debate. Many political and media figures are instrumentalizing the Iranian women’s revolt to justify the claim that Islam is a threat to society.
In Quebec, too, the subject is being discussed. It was above all the statement by Québec solidaire MNA Christine Labrie on September 1 that got people reacting. For her, the ban on wearing the veil in Quebec is also “a form of oppression” – a direct reference to Bill 21, which came into force in June 2019 and prohibits the wearing of religious symbols while providing a government service.
La députée, alors candidate à sa réélect: The MNA, then a candidate for re-election, was vilified by commentators, who argued that the veil is above all “a symbol of oppression,” not a garment one chooses to wear freely. For them, one cannot support the liberation of women in Iran without supporting that of Muslim women in the province through secularism.
Toutefois, pour Mme Kermalli, la réponse: However, for Ms. Kermalli, the answer is clear. “If you support women in Iran, you also support those who want to decide what they wear in their own country. They all have the right to choose.” The lecturer points out that Iranian women are burning their veils mainly because they see it as a symbol of the state. “But in our part of the world, when a woman burns her scarf in Iran, it’s seen as an argument to say: ‘I told you so, it’s a symbol of oppression of Muslim women!’” illustrates the journalist, regretting that a certain Islamophobia may underlie this kind of discourse. Since September 16, hateful acts have in fact targeted the Muslim community in Canada. The <l1>Imam Mahdi mosque in Thornhill, Ontario, was vandalized</l1> and, in Montréal-Nord, <l2>three hate incidents against veiled women took place</l2>.
Même son de cloche du côté de Noroozi, c: Noroozi, a lecturer in philosophy of education and a specialist in questions of colonization and time, sings from the same hymn sheet. Originally from Iran, she grew up in Tehran before settling in Montréal for her studies. “Ideally, I’d like to go back and teach there,” she shares.
Elle rappelle que les manifestantes ne p: She points out that the women protesting are not protesting against the veil, but against the state obligation to wear it. “It’s a symbol. The obligation to wear it is oppressive,” explains the philosopher. In her view, Iran and Quebec cannot be compared, and she believes that banning the veil in Quebec is violent: “Yes, in Quebec, the veil may have been imposed on some Muslim women by their families, but at least they could go out. With a law like Bill 21, choices are taken away from them. Without the veil, they can no longer be in public. It’s a double oppression.”
Et puis, derrière ces réactions médiatiq: And then, behind these media and political reactions, there is a very “colonial” aspect, according to the philosopher. “I’m a specialist in colonization and time, and I don’t use that word lightly! It’s colonial to say we want to see Iranian women free, as if we were freeing them from savagery,” she states. A point of view detailed in various studies, including <l1>the one by journalist Kenza Bennis, published in 2021, on Muslim women in Quebec</l1>: “These women are perceived as being subject to the domination of the men of their culture. The Western media debate thus adopts a paternalistic view and infantilizes these women by not giving them a voice and by speaking in their place.”
« Laissez-nous tranquilles », sont-ils n: “Leave us alone,” many are demanding from Iran. Before our meeting, Nassim asked members of her Twitter community to state their demands to a Canadian media outlet. The wishes of these users echo those of the researchers and the Iranians interviewed for this article.
« Quand je vois d’autres gouvernements c: “When I see other governments criticizing, even though they’re doing no better, I find it hypocritical. I want everyone abroad to stay out of this movement,” says Setareh Sadeqi. She would prefer that, rather than getting into debates, Quebecers and, more broadly, Canadians talk about what concerns them and what they can control. Starting with the sanctions imposed on Iran by countries like the United States and Canada.
Depuis le 3 octobre, Affaires mondiales: Since October 3, Global Affairs Canada has <l1>issued four news releases</l1> announcing the lengthening of the list of individuals and entities sanctioned by Ottawa, meaning they are banned from entering the country or from taking part in transactions. The United States, which has imposed sanctions on Iran since 1979, has done the same, condemning the violation of human rights. “We mustn’t fall into the trap of seeing sanctions as liberating for the population. You can’t reach a democracy under sanctions,” says Nassim.
De son côté, le ministère, contacté par: For its part, the department, contacted by email, simply wrote that “the latest sanctions respond to Iran’s gross human rights violations and ongoing state-sponsored disinformation activities.” Spokesperson Jason Kung did not comment on the call to end the sanctions, but explained that “Canada considers sanctions a complementary tool among other foreign policy tools.”
Nassim et Mme Sadeqi demandent surtout l: Nassim and Ms. Sadeqi above all call for the return of the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) “to truly help the population.” Signed in 2015 by six major powers and Iran, the agreement fell apart after the United States withdrew, a decision made by Donald Trump in 2018. The deal aimed to control Iran’s nuclear program and lift certain economic sanctions. Since 2018, the economic crisis in Iran has worsened, inflation has risen and access to some health care and medication has become more difficult.
Toutes ces sanctions ont aussi des consé: All these sanctions also affect the mobility of Iranian men and women. “Countries like Canada have made travel difficult for Iranian women. It’s also harder to submit to academic journals when the work comes from Iranian scholars,” she denounces.
On peut bien sûr demander à son gouverne: We can of course ask our government to end the sanctions, but beyond that, the women interviewed believe that we above all need to be careful about whom we read, listen to or give a platform to, by examining their affiliations and positions. Checking our sources to avoid disinformation also means questioning the vocabulary and hyperbole used to talk about Iran in general and these protests in particular.
De son côté, Hana exhorte les Canadienne: For her part, Hana urges Canadians to focus on their own struggles. “If you’re a woman in France, Australia or Canada, free yourself from the oppression you tolerate from your own government,” she advises. For her, a politically engaged Canadian is responsible for their government. “We need to educate ourselves about the positions taken by the Canadian government and where they come from,” she continues vehemently, referring to the “problematic” <l1>petition</l1> calling on G7 members to withdraw their embassies from Iran.
Une position qui fait écho au débat sur: A position that echoes the debate over Quebec artists and feminists speaking out. They have been reproached for not taking a position on the situation in Iran. Faced with this attack, feminist and screenwriter Kim Lévesque-Lizotte spoke out on social media and in the media: “As a feminist, I mainly speak out on causes that concern me, that concern society, that I feel I have a handle on, or on injustices,” she told QUB radio. To which Hana responds bluntly: “Don’t worry about me and my country. You don’t know my needs as an Iranian woman. We are here, we know what we need.”
